question.text:
Find the sum modulo $24$ of the solutions to the congruence $20x \equiv 16\:(\text{mod}\:24).$

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=20$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(20,24)=4. \] Since $b=16$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 20x &\equiv 16 && (\text{mod}\:24) \\[3pt] 4\cdot5x &\equiv 4\cdot4 && (\text{mod}\:4\cdot6) \\[3pt] \cancel{4}\cdot5x &\equiv \cancel{4}\cdot4 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel{4}\cdot6) \\[3pt] 5x &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in the new congruence, we have $a_1=5$ and $n_1=6$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(5,6)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $6.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:6).$ To find the inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:6),$ we compute the exponents of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:6)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:6)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 5^2 &\equiv 5\cdot 5 \equiv 25 \equiv 4\cdot 6 + 1 \equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

So, $5 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:6),$ which means that $5$ is its own multiplicative inverse (modulo $6$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $5,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 5x &\equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] 5 \cdot 5x &\equiv 5 \cdot 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] (5 \cdot 5)x &\equiv 20 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 20 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 3\cdot 6 + 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 2 && (\textrm{mod}\:6) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 2 \: (\text{mod}\:6).$

But our original congruence was modulo $24$ (not modulo $6$). To find all the solutions modulo $24,$ we repeatedly add $6$ modulo $24$ until we reach the number $2$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 2 && (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_2&\equiv 2+6 \equiv 8&& (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_3&\equiv 8+6 \equiv 14&& (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_4&\equiv 14+6 \equiv 20&& (\text{mod}\:24) \\[5pt] x_5 &\equiv 20+6 \equiv {26} \equiv 24+2\equiv 2 \equiv x_1&& (\text{mod}\:24) \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv 2, 8, 14, 20 \: (\text{mod}\:24).$

Finally, \[ 2 + 8+14 + 20 \equiv 44 \equiv 24+20\equiv 20 \quad (\text{mod}\:24). \]

example.title: Solving Linear Congruences With Many Solutions

question.text:
Find the sum modulo $33$ of the solutions to the congruence $15x \equiv 18\:(\text{mod}\:33).$

Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=15$ and $n=33$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(15,33)=3. \] Since $b=18$ is divisible by $3,$ our congruence has $3$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 15x &\equiv 18 && (\text{mod}\:33) \\[3pt] 3\cdot5x &\equiv 3\cdot6 && (\text{mod}\:3\cdot11) \\[3pt] \cancel{3}\cdot5x &\equiv \cancel{3}\cdot6 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel{3}\cdot11) \\[3pt] 5x &\equiv 6 && (\text{mod}\:11) \\[3pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in the new congruence above, we have $a_1=5$ and $n_1=11$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(5,11)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $11.$ To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:11).$ And to find the inverse of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:11),$ we compute the exponents of $5\,(\textrm{mod}\:11)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:11)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} 5^2 &\equiv 25 \equiv 2\cdot 11 + 3 \equiv 3 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[3pt] 5^3 &\equiv 3 \cdot 5 \equiv 15 \equiv 11+4 \equiv 4 && (\textrm{mod}\:11)\\[3pt] 5^4 &\equiv 4 \cdot 5 \equiv 20 \equiv 11+9 \equiv 9 && (\textrm{mod}\:11)\\[3pt] 5^5 &\equiv 9 \cdot 5 \equiv 45 \equiv 4\cdot 11 + 1\equiv 1 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \end{align*}

So, $9 \cdot 5 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:11),$ which means that $9$ is the multiplicative inverse of $5$ (modulo $11$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $9,$ we get

\begin{align*} 5x &\equiv 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[3pt] 9 \cdot 5x &\equiv 9 \cdot 6 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[3pt] (9 \cdot 5)x &\equiv 54 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 54 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 4\cdot 11 + 10 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \\[3pt] x &\equiv 10 && (\textrm{mod}\:11) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 10 \: (\text{mod}\:11).$

But our original congruence was modulo $33$ (not modulo $11$). To find all the solutions modulo $33,$ we repeatedly add $11$ modulo $33$ until we reach the number $10$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 10 && (\text{mod}\:33) \\[5pt] x_2&\equiv 10+11 \equiv 21&& (\text{mod}\:33) \\[5pt] x_3&\equiv 21+11 \equiv 32&& (\text{mod}\:33) \\[5pt] x_4 &\equiv 32+11 \equiv {43} \equiv 1\cdot 33+ 10\equiv 10 \equiv x_1&& (\text{mod}\:18) \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv 10, 21, 32 \: (\text{mod}\:33).$

Finally, \[ 10 + 21 + 32 \equiv 63 \equiv 33+30\equiv 30 \quad (\text{mod}\:33). \]

example.title: Solving Linear Congruences With Many Solutions

question.text:
Which of the following congruences have precisely four solutions modulo $24?$

  1. $20x \equiv 6 \quad (\text{mod}\:24)$
  2. $16x \equiv 8 \quad (\text{mod}\:24)$
  3. $28x \equiv 8 \quad (\text{mod}\:24)$
question.explanation:
Recall the following facts regarding the congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n){:}$

  • The congruence has no solutions modulo $n$ if and only if \[ \text{gcd}(a,n) \!\not{|}\:b. \]

  • The congruence has $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)$ solutions modulo $n$ if and only if \[ \text{gcd}(a,n) \:{|}\:b. \]

With that in mind, let's examine our congruences.

  • Congruence I has no solutions. We have $a=20$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(20,24)=4. \] Since $b=6$ is not divisible by $4,$ this congruence has no solutions.

  • Congruence II has eight solutions modulo $24.$ We have $a=16$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(16,24)=8. \] Since $b=8$ is divisible by $8,$ this congruence has $8$ solutions.

  • Congruence III has four solutions modulo $24.$ We have $a=28$ and $n=24$, and so \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(28,24)=4. \] Since $b=8$ is divisible by $4,$ this congruence has $4$ solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

example.title: Identifying Linear Congruences With No Solutions and Many Solutions

question.text:
Find the solutions of $268x \equiv 16 \:(\text{mod}\:404).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $404,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may use the fact that $\text{gcd}(268,404) =4.$
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=268$ and $n=404$, and we're given that \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(268,404)=4. \] Since $b=16$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 268x &\equiv 16 && (\text{mod}\:404) \\[5pt] 4\cdot 67x &\equiv 4\cdot 4 && (\text{mod}\:4\cdot 101) \\[5pt] \cancel 4\cdot 67x &\equiv \cancel 4\cdot 4 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 4\cdot 101) \\[5pt] 67x &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:101) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=67$ and $n_1=101$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(67,101)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $101.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $67\,(\textrm{mod}\:101).$ To find the inverse of $67\,(\textrm{mod}\:101),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} 101 & = & 67\cdot 1 & + & 34 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 34 &=& 101 - 67\cdot 1\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 67 & = &34\cdot 1 & + &33 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 33 &=& 67 - 34\cdot 1\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 34 & = & 33\cdot 1 & + &1 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 1 &=& 34 - 33\cdot 1\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 33 & = & 33\cdot 1 & + &0 \qquad &\phantom\Leftrightarrow&\qquad \phantom 0 &\phantom=&\phantom{14 - 14\cdot 1}\\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

\[ 1 = 2\cdot 101 -3\cdot 67 \]

We can write this result in modulo $101,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 2\cdot 101 -3\cdot 67 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:101)\\[5pt] -3\cdot 67 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:101) \\[5pt] (101-3)\cdot 67 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:101) \\[5pt] 98\cdot 67 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:101) \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse of $67$ modulo $101$ is $98.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $98,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 67x &\equiv 4 && (\text{mod}\:101) \\[5pt] 98\cdot 67x &\equiv 98\cdot 4 && (\text{mod}\:101) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 392 && (\text{mod}\:101) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 101\cdot 3 + 89&& (\text{mod}\:101) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 89 && (\text{mod}\:101) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 89 \: (\text{mod}\:101).$

But our original congruence was modulo $404$ (not modulo $101$). To find all the solutions modulo $404,$ we repeatedly add $101$ to $89$ modulo $404$ until we reach the number $89$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 89 && (\text{mod}\:404) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 89+101 \equiv 190 && (\text{mod}\:404) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 190+101 \equiv 291&& (\text{mod}\:404) \\[5pt] x_4 &\equiv 291+101 \equiv 392&& (\text{mod}\:404) \\[5pt] x_5 &\equiv 392+101 \equiv 493 \equiv 404 + 89 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:404) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2,3,4}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{89}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{190}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{291}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{392} \: (\text{mod}\:404). \]

question.text:
Find the solutions of $92x \equiv 24 \:(\text{mod}\:284).$ Express your answers as nonnegative integers smaller than $284,$ and in ascending order.

Hint: You may use the fact that $\text{gcd}(92,284) =4.$
question.explanation:
In the given congruence, we have $a=92$ and $n=284$, and we're given that \[ \text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(92,284)=4. \] Since $b=24$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

Next, we use the division property of congruences:

\begin{align*} 92x &\equiv 24 && (\text{mod}\:284) \\[5pt] 4\cdot 23x &\equiv 4\cdot 6 && (\text{mod}\:4\cdot 71) \\[5pt] \cancel 4\cdot 23x &\equiv \cancel 4\cdot 6 && (\text{mod}\:\cancel 4\cdot 71) \\[5pt] 23x &\equiv 6 && (\text{mod}\:71) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Notice that in this new congruence, we have $a_1=23$ and $n_1=71$, where \[ \text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(23,71)=1. \] So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $71.$

To find the solution, we must multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $23\,(\textrm{mod}\:71).$ To find the inverse of $23\,(\textrm{mod}\:71),$ we apply the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

\begin{align*} \begin{matrix} 71 & = & 23\cdot 3 & + & 2 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 2 &=& 71 - 23\cdot 3\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 23 & = &11\cdot 2 & + &1 \qquad &\Leftrightarrow&\qquad 1 &=& 23 - 11\cdot 2\\ & \swarrow & & \swarrow & && \\ 11 & = & 11\cdot 1 & + &0 \qquad &\phantom\Leftrightarrow&\qquad \phantom 0 &\phantom=&\phantom{14 - 14\cdot 1}\\ \end{matrix} \end{align*}

Next, back-substituting in the usual way gives the following:

\[ 1 = 34\cdot 23 -11\cdot 71 \]

We can write this result in modulo $71,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} 34\cdot 23 -11\cdot 71 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:71)\\[5pt] 34\cdot 23 &\equiv 1 && (\text{mod}\:71) \end{align*}

Therefore, the inverse of $23$ modulo $71$ is $34.$

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $34,$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} 23x &\equiv 6 && (\text{mod}\:71) \\[5pt] 34\cdot 23x &\equiv 34\cdot 6 && (\text{mod}\:71) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 204 && (\text{mod}\:71) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 71\cdot 2 + 62&& (\text{mod}\:71) \\[5pt] x &\equiv 62 && (\text{mod}\:71) \end{align*}

So, we get the solution $x \equiv 62 \: (\text{mod}\:71).$

But our original congruence was modulo $284$ (not modulo $71$). To find all the solutions modulo $284,$ we repeatedly add $71$ to $62$ modulo $284$ until we reach the number $62$ again:

\begin{align*} x_1 &\equiv 62 && (\text{mod}\:284) \\[5pt] x_2 &\equiv 62+71 \equiv 133 && (\text{mod}\:284) \\[5pt] x_3 &\equiv 133+71 \equiv 204&& (\text{mod}\:284) \\[5pt] x_4 &\equiv 204+71 \equiv 275&& (\text{mod}\:284) \\[5pt] x_5 &\equiv 275+71 \equiv 346 \equiv 284 + 62 \equiv x_1 && (\text{mod}\:284) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are \[ x_{1,2,3,4}\equiv\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{62}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{133}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{204}, \: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{275} \: (\text{mod}\:284). \]
